before.html:
Question 1
?

Solve the inequality 3−x−1<8.

a
x≥1
b
x>3
c
x>1
d
x≤1
e
x<3
Submit

decision.explanation: The square root requires x≥1. On this domain, √(x−1)≥0, so 3−√(x−1)≤3<8. Thus every x≥1 satisfies the inequality.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-\sqrt{x-1} & <8 \\ -\sqrt{x-1} & <5 \\ \sqrt{x-1} & >-5\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we had to flip the sign of the inequality since we divided by a negative number.

Here, the square root is greater than a negative number $(-5),$ so any number we can substitute into the square root will satisfy the inequality. So, the solution is the domain of the square root.

To find the domain, we recall that the expression under the square root must be greater than or equal to $0:$

$$
x-1\ge 0\,⇒\,x\ge 1
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge 1.$

decision.explanation: The square root requires x+3≥0, so x≥−3. On this domain, 4−3√(x+3)≤4≤10, so every x≥−3 satisfies the inequality.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}4-3\sqrt{x+3} & \le 10 \\ -3\sqrt{x+3} & \le 6 \\ \sqrt{x+3} & \ge -2\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we had to flip the sign of the inequality since we divided by a negative number.

Here, the square root is greater than a negative number $(-2),$ so any number we can substitute into the square root will satisfy the inequality. So, the solution is the domain of the square root.

To find the domain, we recall that the expression under the square root must be greater than or equal to $0:$

$$
x+3\ge 0\,⇒\,x\ge -3
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -3.$

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9-2x}-3 & >-4 \\ \sqrt{9-2x} & >-1\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the square root is greater than a negative number $(-1),$ so any number we can substitute into the square root will satisfy the inequality. So, the solution is the domain of the square root.

To find the domain, we recall that the expression under the square root must be greater than or equal to $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-2x & \ge 0 \\ -2x & \ge -9 \\ x & \le \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\le \frac{9}{2}.$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x+2}-4 & >-2 \\ \sqrt{x+2} & >2\end{aligned}
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(2).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{x+2})}^{2} & >{2}^{2} \\ x+2 & >4 \\ x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & \ge 0 \\ x & \ge -2\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x>2,$ which can be expressed as $(2,\infty ).$ The domain of the square root is $x\ge -2,$ which can be expressed as $[-2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
(2,\infty )\cap [-2,\infty )=(2,\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (2,\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>2.$

Question 4
?

Solve the inequality x+2−4>−2.

a
x≥2
b
x>2
c
−4≤x<2
d
x<4
e
−2<x≤4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the square root: x+2−4>−2x+2>2

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number (2). So, we can square both sides of the inequality: (x+2)2>22x+2>4x>2

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero: x+2≥0x≥−2

Our solution is x>2, which can be expressed as (2,∞). The domain of the square root is x≥−2, which can be expressed as [−2,∞). To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection: (2,∞)∩[−2,∞)=(2,∞)

Therefore, the solution is x∈(2,∞), which can also be written as x>2.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms x>2: adding 4 gives √(x+2)>2, and squaring gives x+2>4. All x>2 satisfy the domain x≥−2; x=2 is excluded because it gives equality.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality Involving a Square Root Compared to a Positive Number
content.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x+2}-4 & >-2 \\ \sqrt{x+2} & >2\end{aligned}
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(2).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{x+2})}^{2} & >{2}^{2} \\ x+2 & >4 \\ x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & \ge 0 \\ x & \ge -2\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x>2,$ which can be expressed as $(2,\infty ).$ The domain of the square root is $x\ge -2,$ which can be expressed as $[-2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
(2,\infty )\cap [-2,\infty )=(2,\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (2,\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>2.$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3x-6}-4 & \ge -1 \\ \sqrt{3x-6} & \ge 3\end{aligned}
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(3).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{3x-6})}^{2} & \ge {3}^{2} \\ 3x-6 & \ge 9 \\ 3x & \ge 15 \\ x & \ge 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-6 & \ge 0 \\ 3x & \ge 6 \\ x & \ge 2\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge 5,$ which can be expressed as $[5,\infty ).$ But the domain of the square root is $x\ge 2,$ which can be expressed as $[2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
[5,\infty )\cap [2,\infty )=[5,\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [5,\infty ),$ which can also be written as $5\le x.$
